summaryEn: Hoya travels back to Joseon to learn why King Sejong created 28 new letters in 1443, and how the book Hunminjeongeum explained them in 1446.
learningGoalsEn: Know who created Hangul (King Sejong, the fourth king of Joseon) and when (1443).
Understand why King Sejong made new letters: so ordinary people could learn them easily and write what they wanted to say.
Know that the book Hunminjeongeum (1446) explained the new letters, with explanations written by Jiphyeonjeon scholars.
Read and recognize 세종대왕 (Sejongdaewang), 한자 (hanja), 훈민정음 (Hunminjeongeum), 백성 (baekseong), 집현전 (Jiphyeonjeon) and 한글 (Hangeul).

origin.noteEn: Heritage history, researched from the sources listed on the Sources screen.

scenes.narrationEn: Hoya the tiger opens a glowing storybook. Whoosh! We land in Joseon, Korea, almost 600 years ago. Here lived King Sejong, the fourth king of the Joseon dynasty.

approximations.rationaleEn: King Sejong made the letters in 1443; 1443 to 2026 is 583 years, so narration rounds it to almost 600.

scenes.artBrief: Hoya, a friendly young tiger, steps out of a glowing open book into a Joseon-era royal courtyard with wooden halls and curved tiled roofs; a kind king in royal robes stands on the stone steps.
scenes.captionEn: Hoya lands in King Sejong's Joseon

scenes.narrationEn: In those days, people spoke Korean, but they wrote with Chinese characters. Korean is different from Chinese, and the characters were hard to learn, so many ordinary people could not write down what they wanted to say.
scenes.artBrief: A village lane: a farmer and a child look puzzled at a sheet covered with dense, abstract brush marks (unreadable squiggles, no real characters); Hoya scratches his head beside them.
scenes.captionEn: Chinese characters were hard to learn

scenes.narrationEn: King Sejong felt sorry for them. So, in 1443, he himself created 28 new letters. Hoya's eyes go wide. "Brand-new letters for the sounds of Korean!"
scenes.artBrief: King Sejong at a low wooden desk by lamplight, brush in hand; simple abstract strokes, dots and circles float above the paper like sparks (no readable letters); Hoya peeks over the desk edge.

scenes.narrationEn: He named them Hunminjeongeum, "the proper sounds for teaching the people." An old-fashioned word for the people is {kw:baekseong}. In his own words, he made the letters so people could learn them easily and use them every day.

keyword.en: "the proper sounds for teaching the people"

scenes.artBrief: A sunny market street where a merchant, a grandmother and children each hold a small blank paper and smile; warm light suggests everyone can now write.

scenes.narrationEn: Hoya practices a new phrase: "Baeugi swiwoyo, it's easy to learn!" Later, the scholar Jeong Inji wrote that a wise person could understand the letters before a single morning was over.
scenes.artBrief: Morning sun rising over palace roofs; Hoya sits cross-legged with a brush and blank paper, grinning proudly; a scholar in a black gat hat watches kindly.
scenes.captionEn: The new letters are easy to learn

scenes.narrationEn: In 1446, a book named Hunminjeongeum was finished to explain the new letters. Scholars of the royal Hall of Worthies, Jiphyeonjeon, wrote its explanations and examples.

keyword.en: the Hall of Worthies (the king's hall of scholars)

scenes.artBrief: Several scholars in Joseon robes working at desks in a quiet wooden hall, stacks of bound books with plain covers; one scholar holds up a finished book (cover blank, no text).
scenes.captionEn: Scholars explain the letters in a book

scenes.narrationEn: Today we call these letters Hangul. People in Korea read and write with them every day, and now you are learning them too!
scenes.artBrief: Present-day scene: Hoya waves beside a child holding a pencil over a notebook (blank lines), with a modern Korean street softly behind them; no signs or readable text.

facts.claimEn: Before Hangeul, Korean was written with borrowed Chinese characters. Because Korean differs from Chinese and the characters were hard to learn, many ordinary people could not write down what they wanted to say.

facts.claimEn: In 1443 (recorded in the 12th lunar month of Sejong's 25th year), King Sejong himself created 28 letters and called them Hunminjeongeum.
facts.claimKo: 1443년(세종 25년 음력 12월 조 기록)에 세종이 친히 언문 28자를 만들고, 이를 훈민정음이라 하였다.

facts.claimEn: In his preface, King Sejong wrote that he felt sorry for people who could not express themselves, and that he made 28 new letters so people could learn them easily and use them conveniently every day.
facts.claimKo: 세종은 서문에서 제 뜻을 펴지 못하는 백성을 딱하게 여겨 새로 28자를 만들었으며, 사람들이 쉽게 익혀 날마다 편하게 쓰게 하려는 것이라고 밝혔다.

sources.title: 세종실록 113권, 세종 28년 9월 29일 갑오 4번째 기사 「《훈민정음》이 이루어지다. 어제와 예조 판서 정인지의 서문」 (1446, 명 정통 11년)

facts.claimEn: Jeong In-ji's preface to Hunminjeongeum says that a wise person can understand the letters before a morning is over.
facts.claimKo: 정인지는 『훈민정음』 서문에서 지혜로운 사람은 아침나절이 되기 전에 이 글자를 깨칠 수 있다고 썼다.

sources.title: 세종실록 113권, 세종 28년 9월 29일 갑오 4번째 기사 「《훈민정음》이 이루어지다. 어제와 예조 판서 정인지의 서문」 (1446, 명 정통 11년)

facts.claimEn: In the 9th lunar month of 1446, the book Hunminjeongeum, which explains the new letters, was completed. UNESCO and the Korea Heritage Service describe it as published (promulgated) in 1446, but no formal promulgation ceremony is recorded.

verification.notes: Third independent pass. Every cited URL for all 6 episodes (52 facts) was re-opened (UNESCO pages via Wayback copies when the live site resets connections) and quotes/locators were compared; the one exception is unesco.org/en/prizes/literacy (unreachable from here; its claim is now also backed by a Korean MCST press release). Eight minimal corrections were made: (1) Hangeul Day f3 no longer says 'Gregorian' (no cited source says the October 9 conversion was Gregorian; encykorea separates Julian/Gregorian only for 1932-45) and dates the October 29/28 observances; (2) f10 gains a third source (SBS 2018 with 국립한글박물관 curator); (3) Shapes scene 8, learning goal and f7 now say 'South Korea's spelling rules' count 24 (North Korea counts 40, 국립한글박물관 webzine 59); (4) Sejong scene 4/f4: 백성 is 'an old-fashioned word' with 표준국어대사전 added; (5) Jikji f8 quote no longer repeats a prize amount that differs between UNESCO page versions; (6) Tripitaka f6 wood and corner plates now have two further sources (정책브리핑; 박상진 wood-identification study); (8) Hangeul Day f9 gains a second source (문화체육관광부 press release); (7) Panjeon scene 8/f9: 'visitors cannot walk inside' replaced by 'visitor entry is restricted' because Haeinsa has run pre-booked tours inside Beopbojeon since June 2021. See hangul-printing.signoff.md.

authorNotes: Revised after two independent checks. 'Promulgation' wording removed from the narration and summary: the Sillok 1446/9 entry only records that Hunminjeongeum was completed ('是月, 訓民正音成'), and 국립국어원 says no official promulgation ceremony is recorded and that a September 1446 promulgation is unsupported; UNESCO, 국가유산포털 and 국립한글박물관 do use 'published/promulgated 1446', so f7 states both. Scene 2 now gives both reasons from Sejong's preface (Korean differs from Chinese; the characters were hard to learn). Scene 5 phrase fixed to 배우기 쉬워요 (baeugi swiwoyo, 'it's easy to learn'). The word 백성 now appears in scene 4 narration; scene 6 key word is 집현전. The 1443 and 1446 Sillok entries are month-end entries in the lunar calendar with no specific day (the 12th lunar month of Sejong 25 falls in early 1444 in the Gregorian calendar, but UNESCO, 국가유산포털 and encykorea all say 1443, so the story follows that convention). Scene 5 quotes only the first half of Jeong In-ji's line. The 'almost 600 years ago' wording is worked out from 1443. The companion 훈이 ('Sejong's cat' in BP04) was deliberately not used. Illustrations must not show a proclamation ceremony. Do not name a specific palace or a royal robe colour. f9: the 표준국어대사전 quotation could not be read (dynamic page) and was replaced by the UNESCO wording ('now called han-gul'); the 한국민족문화대백과사전 한글 entry also states the point. The 국가유산포털 description text quoted in f1, f7, f8 was re-read from the portal's description fragment (hub_img/html/cul_1111100700000) in the research folder. FINAL PASS (3rd check): scene 4 now says 'An old-fashioned word for the people is baekseong' and f4 cites 표준국어대사전 for 백성. All other facts re-verified unchanged. REVIEW PASS (PR 1.8b): learner prose writes the scholar's name Jeong Inji (F-CNT-002 rule 8); f6 and f8 keep the researched spelling Jeong In-ji. Check c3 options rebalanced so the answer is not the longest.
